sections.title: A country for seven years, and a prime minister for a day
sections.intro_md:
On the morning of 11 August 1961 an Indian civil servant named K. G. Badlani woke up as the prime minister of a small country. By evening he had signed it away. The country was Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli: about 490 square km of teak forest and Adivasi villages between Gujarat and Maharashtra, which had thrown out its Portuguese police in 1954 and then waited seven years, in legal limbo, while Portugal and India argued about it in The Hague.

That odd episode is the key to today's union territory. **Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu** is not a natural region. It is four leftover fragments of **Portuguese India**, the empire that held parts of India's west coast for over four centuries, glued into one unit in 2020. Two pieces are forest and factories inland. Two are old fortified ports on the sea. Their story runs from a 1509 naval battle that decided who would control the Indian Ocean, to a 2018 island that runs on sunlight.

spotlights.name: Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli
spotlights.spot_it: No flag of its own and no foreign recognition: a strip of forest villages run by a council called the Varishta Panchayat, cut off from Portugal and not yet part of India.
spotlights.story_md: For seven years about 490 square km of Adivasi forest villages was, in practice, its own country. Volunteers took Dadra on the night of 21 to 22 July 1954 and Silvassa by 2 August; the Portuguese police fled. India did not annex it. Lisbon was suing in the World Court, and Delhi wanted to look patient. So a local council, the **Varishta Panchayat of Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli**, ran the territory until 1961. To end it neatly, India sent a Gujarat-cadre IAS officer, **K. G. Badlani**. On 11 August 1961 he was named prime minister of the little state for a single day, long enough to sign its merger agreement with Jawaharlal Nehru.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how India absorbed the last colonial enclaves: slowly, legally, and with a lot of improvisation.
spotlights.memory_hook: A one-day prime minister signed his own country out of existence.

spotlights.name: Right of Passage over Indian Territory (Portugal v. India)
spotlights.spot_it: A World Court judgment you will find in every international-law textbook, about whether Portuguese soldiers could cross 20 km of India to reach two landlocked villages.
spotlights.story_md: Portugal argued that it had a right, built on Maratha-era practice and treaties, to march officials and troops across Indian soil to its enclaves. India blocked the road after July 1954. The International Court of Justice split the question in two. By **11 votes to 4** it found that Portugal did have a right of passage for private people, civil officials and goods. By just **8 votes to 7** it found that the right did not cover armed forces, armed police or weapons. By 9 to 6 it said India had not broken the law by stopping the passage. Both sides claimed victory; Dadra and Nagar Haveli stayed exactly where they were.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the classic case for the idea that a custom between just two countries can be binding law.
spotlights.memory_hook: One vote decided that soldiers could not walk to Silvassa.

sections.title: Three districts that do not touch
sections.intro_md:
The territory covers just **603 square km** and had about **5.87 lakh** people in 2011. It has three districts. **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** (491 square km) is inland: a big C-shaped enclave wrapped around a small Gujarati village, plus the tiny separate enclave of Dadra. **Daman** (72 square km) is a coastal enclave on Gujarat's southern edge. **Diu** (40 square km) is an island off the south coast of Saurashtra, about 200 km to the west across the Gulf of Khambhat.

The capital is **Daman**; the largest town is **Silvassa**. Hindi and Gujarati are official, and you will also hear Marathi, Varli, Konkani and a Portuguese creole. About 92% of people are Hindu, 5.5% Muslim and 1.3% Christian. The UT sends **two MPs** to the Lok Sabha, falls under the **Bombay High Court**, and has no legislature: an administrator appointed by the President runs it.

spotlights.name: The merger of 2020
spotlights.spot_it: One administrator, one police force, one seal, three districts that do not touch: Dadra and Nagar Haveli inland, Daman on the coast, Diu island about 200 km to the west.
spotlights.story_md: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu had shared an administrator and officers for years, but still ran as two separate territories. In July 2019 the Centre proposed joining them to cut duplication. The **merger bill** was introduced on 26 November 2019, signed by the President on 9 December, and took effect on **Republic Day 2020**. India went from nine union territories to eight. The new UT has its capital at Daman, though its biggest town, Silvassa, lies about 25 km inland. It sends two MPs to the Lok Sabha and falls under the Bombay High Court. It has no legislature of its own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare case of India reducing the number of its territories to save money.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three pieces that never touch, glued together on Republic Day.

sections.title: River, forest, creek and coast
sections.intro_md:
The two halves of the territory are two different landscapes. Inland, **Nagar Haveli** lies on the western foothills of the Sahyadri, the Western Ghats, from near sea level up to 425 m. It is a country of low teak-covered hills, rice valleys and the wide **Damanganga** river, with roughly two-fifths of the land under forest. The monsoon here is heavy: Daman, on the same river's mouth, gets about 1,900 mm a year, almost all of it from June to September.

On the coast, **Daman** is flat, sandy and tidal, with grey beaches and big mud flats. **Diu** is different again: a dry limestone island with only about 850 mm of rain, rocky shores full of tide pools, and a mangrove creek that separates it from Gujarat. Two living things say a lot about the history: flamingos that winter in that creek, and an odd branching palm that may have come from Africa on Portuguese ships.

spotlights.name: The Damanganga river
spotlights.spot_it: A wide brown monsoon river that runs past Silvassa, under the bridges of Vapi, and out to sea between the two forts of Daman.
spotlights.story_md: The river is the thread that ties the two mainland pieces together. It rises at about 950 m near Ambegaon in Nashik district, in the Sahyadri hills, and runs **131 km** west to the Arabian Sea. On the way it passes through Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Silvassa, crosses Gujarat, and ends at Daman, where it splits the town into **Moti Daman** (big Daman, the walled south bank) and **Nani Daman** (little Daman, the north bank). Its catchment covers about 2,330 square km in two states and the UT. Upstream, the Madhuban dam in Valsad district stores water shared between Gujarat and the territory.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without this river there would be no Daman harbour, no Silvassa water supply and no factories.
spotlights.memory_hook: Big Daman, little Daman, and a river between them.

spotlights.name: Dadra and Nagar Haveli Wildlife Sanctuary
spotlights.spot_it: Teak and mixed dry forest in the Sahyadri foothills, with chital, nilgai and chinkara at Satmaliya and a small lion safari at Vasona.
spotlights.story_md: Nagar Haveli sits on the western foothills of the Western Ghats, and roughly two-fifths of the territory around Silvassa is under forest. The sanctuary covers about **97 square km**. Its best-known corners are made for visitors: **Satmaliya deer park** near Khanvel, home to chital, blackbuck and chinkara with more than 100 bird species recorded, and the **Vasona lion safari** about 10 km from Silvassa, a fenced enclosure of some 20 acres built to keep Asiatic lions. The wilder forest holds peafowl, flamebacks, pythons and the green vine snake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the green buffer between India's fastest-growing factory belt and the hills.
spotlights.memory_hook: Deer in the morning, smokestacks on the horizon.

spotlights.name: Fudam bird sanctuary
spotlights.spot_it: Mangroves and mudflats in the creek between Diu island and Gujarat, with pink flamingos wading in winter.
spotlights.story_md: Diu is an island because of a narrow tidal creek, and that creek is now its bird sanctuary. The forest department describes it as about **245 hectares** of mangrove wetland between the island and Gujarat; first proposed in 1991, it was notified in **2006**. Flamingos arrive in winter, known locally as **surkhaab**, along with gulls, herons and waders. A 2025 count listed about 108 species; the forest department claims more than 200 over the years. You see it best by boat, early in the morning, before the tide and the heat flatten everything.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns the strip of water that makes Diu an island into a refuge.
spotlights.memory_hook: The creek that cut Diu loose now feeds flamingos.

spotlights.name: Hoka palm
spotlights.spot_it: A palm that does something palms are not supposed to do: its trunk forks into two, then four, then eight, like a candelabra, with fan-shaped leaves.
spotlights.story_md: Most palms grow one straight stem. The **hoka** of Diu branches. INTACH's heritage record calls it the only Indian form of the doum palm, a tree native to the Nile valley and northern Kenya, and says the Portuguese brought it from Africa and that in India it grows only in Diu. Botanists are less tidy about it. Some identify Diu's trees as *Hyphaene dichotoma*, a species they consider native to the coasts of Gujarat and Maharashtra. Either way the forked silhouettes along Diu's roads are its signature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tree that may record five centuries of Portuguese sailing between Africa and India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The palm that forks: Diu's candelabra tree.

sections.title: Diu, where the Indian Ocean changed hands
sections.intro_md:
Before the Portuguese came, Diu was one of the busiest ports of the **Sultanate of Gujarat**, trading with the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf under its governor **Malik Ayyaz**. The Portuguese wanted Diu more than any other port in Gujarat, because whoever held it could watch the shipping lanes to Arabia.

In under forty years Diu saw four great fights. A Portuguese fleet smashed the combined navies of Egypt, Gujarat and Calicut in its harbour in **1509**. A sultan of Gujarat let the Portuguese build a fort there in **1535** and died off its shore in **1537**. An Ottoman armada, the furthest east that empire ever sent a fleet in force, besieged it in **1538**. And Gujarat tried again in **1546**. Each time the Portuguese held. These are the reasons a town in Saurashtra appears in Turkish, Portuguese and Mughal history books.

spotlights.name: Battle of Diu, 1509
spotlights.spot_it: Portuguese carracks firing broadsides into a harbour packed with Mamluk galleys and Gujarati ships under the walls of Diu.
spotlights.story_md: This is one of the turning points of world history, and it happened off a town most Indians have never visited. The Portuguese viceroy **Francisco de Almeida** came for revenge: his son Lourenço had been killed by a Mamluk Egyptian fleet at Chaul in 1508. At Diu that fleet sat with the ships of the Sultan of Gujarat and the Zamorin of Calicut, under Diu's governor **Malik Ayyaz**. Almeida had about 18 ships against more than 100 vessels, but his carracks carried heavy guns. The coalition lost every Mamluk ship; the Portuguese lost 32 dead. Almeida executed most of his prisoners.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave Portugal control of the Indian Ocean trade routes for about a century.
spotlights.memory_hook: A father's revenge won Portugal an ocean.

spotlights.name: Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
spotlights.spot_it: In the Akbarnama painting he is a small figure tumbling from a boat into a sea full of Portuguese ships.
spotlights.story_md: Bahadur Shah let the Portuguese into Diu because he was losing a war on land. In 1535 the Mughal emperor Humayun chased him out of Champaner and across Gujarat. Desperate for guns and allies, he signed treaties that gave Portugal Bassein (Vasai) and permission to build a fort at Diu. Once the Mughals left, he tried to get rid of his new guests. In February 1537 he went aboard a Portuguese ship to negotiate. On the way back there was a scuffle, and the sultan died in the water. Each side blamed the other, and Mughal court painters made it a scene.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His death left the Portuguese in Diu for the next 424 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: He invited the Portuguese in and drowned trying to get them out.

spotlights.name: The Ottoman siege of 1538
spotlights.spot_it: Old prints show a tiny fort ringed by an Ottoman fleet, cannon smoke, and an army breaking off and running.
spotlights.story_md: The Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent sent his governor of Egypt, **Hadim Suleiman Pasha**, a eunuch of about 60, to throw the Portuguese out of India. He arrived with somewhere between 70 and 80 ships and thousands of men and joined a Gujarati army outside Diu. Inside were about **600 Portuguese** under António da Silveira, plus civilians. The siege lasted about four months. Then, with the walls battered but still standing, the pasha gave up and sailed home. The Ottomans never again sent an armada that size to India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the furthest east the Ottoman navy ever pushed in force.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six hundred men and one fort stopped an empire.

spotlights.name: João de Castro and the siege of 1546
spotlights.spot_it: A stern Portuguese governor in armour, painted on the walls of the old museum at Goa, the man who saved Diu a second time.
spotlights.story_md: Eight years later Gujarat tried again. **Khoja Zafar**, a commander of Ottoman origin in Gujarati service, besieged Diu for seven months; he and his son were both killed in the fighting. The defence held under João de Mascarenhas until the governor of Portuguese India, **João de Castro**, sailed up with a relief fleet and routed the besiegers. A famous story, told by his 17th century biographer, says Castro had no money to rebuild the broken fort and pledged hairs from his own beard to the merchants of Goa as security for a loan. Whether or not it happened, the fort was rebuilt.
spotlights.why_it_matters: After 1546 nobody seriously challenged Portuguese Diu until 1961.
spotlights.memory_hook: He pawned his beard to rebuild a fort, or so the story goes.

sections.title: The forts that never fell to a siege
sections.intro_md:
Portuguese power in India was built on stone: small, heavily armed forts at river mouths and on islands, supplied by sea, that could hold out for months against much bigger armies on land. The territory has some of the best surviving examples anywhere.

At **Diu**, the great fort fills the eastern tip of the island, with the sea on three sides and a double moat cut into the rock on the fourth. A little water fort, **Panikota**, sits in the channel opposite. The old town behind them was walled, and its gates still stand. At **Daman**, the Portuguese built two forts facing each other across the Damanganga: **Moti Daman**, a whole walled town of about 84 acres with ten bastions, and the smaller **Fort of St Jerome** on the north bank. Every ship entering the river had to pass between them. None of these forts fell to a siege. They fell in 1961 to aircraft.

spotlights.name: Diu Fort
spotlights.spot_it: A huge pale sandstone fort at the eastern tip of the island, washed by the sea on three sides, with a double moat cut into rock on the fourth and a lighthouse on top.
spotlights.story_md: The fort was thrown up in a few months between 1535 and 1536 under the treaty with Bahadur Shah, and thickened after each siege until 1546. It is built of sandstone and lime. A **double moat**, the outer one tidal, separates it from the town, and on the walls you still find bronze cannon. The fort survived two great sieges, then came under Indian air attack in December 1961, when rockets set a fire near the munitions store and the garrison evacuated. Today it is Diu's most visited sight, with a working lighthouse and a sub-jail block inside the walls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest and best-preserved Portuguese forts anywhere in Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sea on three sides, a moat on the fourth, 426 years under one flag.

spotlights.name: Panikota (Fortim do Mar)
spotlights.spot_it: A small stone fort sitting in the middle of the channel facing Diu Fort, shaped like a ship at anchor, glowing in the evening light.
spotlights.story_md: Facing Diu Fort, on a rock in the harbour mouth, stands **Panikota**, the water fort, also called the Fortim do Mar. It guarded the channel, carried a light, and later served as a prison, which is why locals and photographers call it the sea jail. From the ramparts of the main fort it looks like a ship riding at anchor. It can be reached only by boat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It completes the pair of forts that locked Diu's harbour shut for four centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fort that looks like a ship and worked like a jail.

spotlights.name: Moti Daman fort
spotlights.spot_it: A wide walled rectangle on the south bank of the Damanganga with ten arrow-shaped bastions, two carved gates, and government offices and churches inside.
spotlights.story_md: Constantino de Bragança, viceroy of Portuguese India, sailed in and took Daman from Gujarat's Abyssinian commander on 2 February 1559. The Portuguese then built a walled town of about **84 acres** with **ten bastions**, finished by 1593 according to the inscription on the north gate. Unlike Diu Fort, this was not just a citadel but a whole town: streets, houses, convents and churches inside the wall. It still works that way. Government offices, including the territory's secretariat, and the Bom Jesus church are inside, so officials drive through 16th century gates to get to work.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Few capitals anywhere run their government from inside a working 16th century fortress.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten bastions, two gates, and a secretariat inside.

spotlights.name: Fort of St Jerome, Nani Daman
spotlights.spot_it: A smaller fort across the river, its gate topped by a statue of St Jerome with two huge human figures standing guard on either side.
spotlights.story_md: Across the Damanganga from Moti Daman, the Portuguese built a second, smaller fort to guard the north bank and the river mouth. It is named after **St Jerome**, whose statue stands above the main gate between two giant figures. Inside is the little **Church of Our Lady of the Sea** and a Portuguese cemetery. The two forts face each other across the estuary, so any ship entering the river sailed between them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: With its twin across the water it made Daman a fortified river mouth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two forts, one river, no way in.

spotlights.name: Zampa gateway
spotlights.spot_it: A carved town gate in Diu's old wall, with lions, angels and a priest in stone, painted bright colours.
spotlights.story_md: Diu town was walled on its landward side, and **Zampa** is its most decorated surviving gate. The carvings show lions, angels and a priest, and inside the gateway is a small chapel. Walk through it and you enter the lanes of the old town, with painted houses, Portuguese balconies and small chapels on street corners.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the front door of one of India's most intact colonial small towns.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lions, angels and a chapel in a doorway.

sections.title: How the inland villages became Portuguese, and stopped being
sections.intro_md:
Daman and Diu were seized by force in the 16th century. **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** came much later and much more strangely. In the 1770s the Portuguese were weak and the Marathas strong, and the two quarrelled over a damaged Portuguese warship. To settle it, the Peshwa's government handed over the revenues of 72 villages inland from Daman. Portugal took possession of **Nagar Haveli in 1783** and **Dadra in 1785**, and governed them for 171 years from Daman, across a strip of British, and later Indian, territory.

That strip was the enclaves' weakness. After independence, India pressed Portugal to leave Goa, Daman and Diu, and Portugal refused. In July 1954 India closed the road. Within weeks a mixed band of Goan nationalists, RSS volunteers, Communist-led Warli peasants and Indian police had pushed the Portuguese out without a single army unit crossing the border.

spotlights.name: How Nagar Haveli became Portuguese
spotlights.spot_it: Not a conquest at all: 72 inland villages handed over by the Marathas to settle a quarrel about one damaged ship.
spotlights.story_md: Portugal never fought for Dadra and Nagar Haveli. In 1772 the Maratha navy damaged, or by some accounts captured, the Portuguese frigate **Santana**. Under a friendship treaty of 17 December 1779 the Peshwa's government agreed to compensate Portugal with the revenue of a group of villages. Portugal took possession of Nagar Haveli, about 72 villages, on 10 June 1783 and added Dadra in 1785. Some popular histories say the Marathas meant it as temporary, and simply never asked for the land back. Portugal held it for 171 years, with no coast and no road of its own to reach it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A ship accident drew a border that India's map still shows.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seventy-two villages, the price of one frigate.

spotlights.name: The fall of Dadra and Silvassa, 1954
spotlights.spot_it: No battle and almost no army: a raid on a police post at night, a flag raised at dawn, and a Portuguese captain walking his men into India to surrender.
spotlights.story_md: Once India closed the roads, the enclaves were defenceless. On the night of 21 to 22 July 1954 the **United Front of Goans**, led by Francis Mascarenhas and Viman Sardesai, attacked the Dadra police station; a Portuguese inspector was killed and an Indian flag went up in the morning. Days later RSS volunteers and fighters of the Azad Gomantak Dal took the post at Naroli, and Warli protesters marched into villages near Luhari. The Portuguese police abandoned Silvassa. Their commander, Captain Virgílio Fidalgo, retreated with about 150 men into the forest and surrendered to Indian police on 11 August.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first piece of Portuguese India to fall, seven years before Goa.
spotlights.memory_hook: A police station, a flag and a walk into the forest.

sections.title: 1961, 1971 and the sea
sections.intro_md:
Goa, Daman and Diu fell together in **Operation Vijay**, on 18 and 19 December 1961. Daman was taken by the Maratha Light Infantry in about a day. Diu, an island with a strong garrison and a narrow creek, needed the air force and a cruiser. Portugal refused to accept any of it until its own revolution in 1974; a treaty signed in New Delhi on **31 December 1974** finally recognised Indian sovereignty over all the former territories. From 1962 Daman and Diu were run together with Goa, and when Goa became a state in 1987 they were left as a separate union territory.

Ten years after liberation, the war of 1971 brought the Navy's darkest night to Diu's waters. The sinking of **INS Khukri** and the conduct of her captain are commemorated on a hill above the sea at Diu, now one of the island's most visited places.

visual.title: Operation Vijay: the two garrisons, December 1961

spotlights.name: Operation Vijay at Diu
spotlights.spot_it: An old cruiser offshore, jets over the fort, and a small patrol boat that chose to fight.
spotlights.story_md: Diu was defended by about 400 soldiers and police under Major Fernando de Almeida e Vasconcelos. Indian infantry attacks across the creek on 18 December were beaten back, so the air force went in: jets cut the runway and rockets started a fire near the fort's munitions store. Offshore, the cruiser **INS Delhi** shelled shore targets. She had been HMS Achilles, one of three British cruisers that fought the German pocket battleship **Graf Spee** at the River Plate in 1939. The patrol boat NRP Vega fired at Indian aircraft and was sunk; its commander and a gunner died. Diu surrendered on 19 December.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended 426 years of Portuguese rule in Diu in about a day and a half.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Second World War cruiser closed a 16th century fort.

spotlights.name: The fall of Daman, 1961
spotlights.spot_it: A freedom memorial inside the walls of Moti Daman marks where the last Portuguese governor of Daman was carried out to surrender.
spotlights.story_md: Daman's governor, Major António José da Costa Pinto, had about 360 soldiers, 200 police and 30 customs men. The 1st Battalion, Maratha Light Infantry attacked from 4 a.m. on 18 December; Indian Mystère jets flew 14 sorties. The next morning at 11 the Portuguese surrendered at the airfield. Costa Pinto, wounded, had to be carried there. About 600 men were taken prisoner. India lost 4 dead and the Portuguese 10. Daman's patrol boat escaped and reached Karachi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Daman's liberation day, 19 December, is still a public holiday in the territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wounded governor, carried to surrender on a stretcher.

spotlights.name: INS Khukri memorial
spotlights.spot_it: A scale model of a grey frigate inside a glass case on a seaside hill, facing the stretch of water where the real ship lies.
spotlights.story_md: On the night of 9 December 1971, during the war with Pakistan, the Indian frigate **Khukri** was at sea off Diu. The Pakistani submarine **PNS Hangor** fired a torpedo that hit beneath her oil tanks, and she sank about 35 miles south-west of Diu harbour. **18 officers and 176 sailors** died, the Indian Navy's worst single loss of life since independence. The memorial on a hill at Diu holds a scale model of the ship in glass and an open-air amphitheatre looking out to sea.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Navy's main memorial to its costliest night.
spotlights.memory_hook: 194 men, one night, and a glass ship on a hill.

spotlights.name: Captain Mahendra Nath Mulla
spotlights.spot_it: A bronze bust of a calm, moustached naval officer; on the 2000 stamp, the frigate behind him.
spotlights.story_md: Khukri's commanding officer, **Captain Mahendra Nath Mulla**, stayed with his ship as she went down. Survivors' accounts say he helped men off and gave away his own life jacket. He is the only Indian captain to have gone down with his ship. He was awarded the **Maha Vir Chakra**, India's second-highest gallantry award, after his death. Films Division made a short film about him, India Post issued a stamp in 2000, and a naval auditorium carries his name and his bust.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave India its clearest example of a captain's last duty.
spotlights.memory_hook: The captain who stayed with his ship.

sections.title: Churches, a sea temple and a Jain shrine
sections.intro_md:
Most people in the territory are Hindu, and its landscape of faith is mostly temples and village shrines. But the Portuguese left a cluster of churches that are among the finest outside Goa. In Diu, three great churches stand within a few hundred metres: **St Paul's**, still in use, **St Thomas**, now the museum, and **St Francis of Assisi**, which became a hospital. In Daman the churches of **Bom Jesus**, the **Rosary** and **Our Lady of Remedios** are inside or near the forts.

Other faiths are just as visible. Daman has an 18th century **Jain temple** with murals; Diu has a Parsi tower of silence, mosques, and the sea temple of **Gangeshwar**, where the tide washes over five Shiva lingas. The Adivasi villages of Nagar Haveli keep their own gods: a mother goddess and the spirits of field and forest, honoured with the dances you will meet in the next section.

spotlights.name: St Paul's Church, Diu
spotlights.spot_it: A dazzling white baroque facade with scrolls, shells and empty niches, taller than anything around it in the old town.
spotlights.story_md: Jesuits laid the foundation stone on 7 April 1601, and the church was completed in 1610 and dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception. Its facade is often compared to Goa's Bom Jesus basilica, and some writers think it is the finer piece of work: deep volutes, shell motifs and a richly carved wooden interior. Of the three great churches of old Diu it is the only one still used as a church. The other two have changed jobs: St Thomas is a museum, and St Francis of Assisi became a hospital.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the showpiece of Portuguese baroque north of Goa.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three churches, three jobs: prayer, museum, hospital.

spotlights.name: St Thomas Church museum, Diu
spotlights.when: Church of the Portuguese era, now a museum
spotlights.spot_it: A plain white church whose nave is filled not with pews but with carved saints, stone inscriptions and old statues.
spotlights.story_md: When the Portuguese left, Diu's Catholic population was too small to fill three big churches. **St Thomas** became the Diu museum, displaying wooden saints, stone carvings, inscriptions and sculpture gathered from the island's history. Next door, the **Church of St Francis of Assisi**, built in 1593, was turned into a hospital. Walking between them gives a quick lesson in how a town re-uses the buildings of a departed power instead of pulling them down.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps the island's scattered heritage in one hall.
spotlights.memory_hook: A church full of saints and no congregation.

spotlights.name: Church of Bom Jesus, Moti Daman
spotlights.spot_it: A white church inside the walls of Moti Daman, with a carved stone doorway lined with statues of saints and a gilded altar.
spotlights.story_md: Daman's Bom Jesus is a different building from the famous basilica in Goa, but it is about as old. The government tourism page says the church was founded with the conquest of 1559 and consecrated in 1603. Its doorway carries carved figures of six saints, and the gilded 17th century altar holds painted statues of saints in arches. It still serves Daman's Catholic families, many of whom keep Portuguese surnames and speak the local Portuguese creole at home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It anchors Daman's living Catholic community.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not Goa's Bom Jesus: Daman's own, nearly as old.

spotlights.name: Jain temple, Daman
spotlights.spot_it: White marble, quiet halls, and walls covered with 18th century murals and reliefs of dancing women.
spotlights.story_md: Daman's trading families were not only Catholic. An 18th century **Jain temple** dedicated to Mahavira, built in white marble, has murals of the same century on its walls, and carved reliefs of dancers. It is a reminder that under the Portuguese many of the town's merchants were Gujarati Jains and Hindus, who worshipped a few streets away from the churches.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the Gujarati merchant world that actually ran colonial Daman's trade.
spotlights.memory_hook: Murals of Mahavira a few streets from Bom Jesus.

sections.title: The Adivasi heartland
sections.intro_md:
Strip away the factories and Dadra and Nagar Haveli is an Adivasi country. In the early 1980s Scheduled Tribes were about three-quarters of its people; in 2011, after three decades of migration, they were still about **52%** of the district, some 1.79 lakh people. The **Warli** (Varli) are the largest group, followed by the Kokna, Dhodia, Dubla (Halpati), Kathodi, Koli and others.

Their year turns on rice and the monsoon. After the harvest come the dances: the **tarpa**, danced in a long human chain around a gourd horn, the **tur and thali** with clay drum and brass plate, the **bhawada** at Holi, and the masked **Bohada** in spring. The administration now runs a yearly Tarpa festival in Silvassa, but the dances still belong first to village nights. In 1954 these same villagers marched against the Portuguese,, alongside Goan nationalists and RSS volunteers.

visual.title: Dadra and Nagar Haveli: population and Scheduled Tribes

spotlights.name: The Warli of Nagar Haveli
spotlights.when: Largest community of the inland district
spotlights.spot_it: Thatched houses with mud walls painted in white stick figures, rice fields in the valleys, and a ring of dancers around a horn player after harvest.
spotlights.story_md: Before the factories, Dadra and Nagar Haveli belonged to its Adivasi communities: the **Warli** (Varli), Kokna, Dhodia, Dubla, Kathodi and others. The Linguistic Survey of India found that in the 1991 census Varli was the mother tongue of **48.87%** of the territory's people, by far the largest. The Warli live across the border region of Maharashtra and Gujarat as well, from Palghar to Valsad. They farm rice and millet, honour a mother goddess and nature spirits, and are famous for two things: their wall painting and the tarpa dance. In 1954 Warli marchers were part of the uprising against Portuguese rule.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the original people of the territory and still its largest single community.
spotlights.memory_hook: A language spoken by half the territory in 1991, and written by no one.

spotlights.name: Tarpa and the tarpa dance
spotlights.spot_it: A long, curved horn made from a dried gourd, with a droning, nasal sound; dancers hold each other by the waist and coil around the player.
spotlights.story_md: The **tarpa** is a wind instrument made from a dried bottle gourd, palm leaves, bamboo and wax. Its player stands in the middle while men and women, arms around each other's waists, form a chain that snakes and spirals around him, changing direction with the tune. It is danced at night in the season after the monsoon harvest by Warli, Kokna and Koli villagers. The same circle of dancers around a tarpa player is one of the commonest images in Warli painting. Every year the UT administration runs a **Tarpa festival** to show it off.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the sound and shape of Adivasi celebration in the territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gourd horn, and a human chain that coils around it.

spotlights.name: Bohada mask festival

where.label: Kokna and Warli villages, Nagar Haveli and Palghar

spotlights.spot_it: Night-long dancing in huge painted wooden masks of gods and demons, lit by torches, with drums and horns.
spotlights.story_md: **Bohada** is the masked festival of the Kokna, Warli and Mahadeo Koli communities on both sides of the Maharashtra border, held in spring around the month of Chaitra. Dancers wear big carved and painted masks of Ganesha, goddesses and many lesser spirits, and act out myths through the night. Families keep the masks for generations, and they are purified with turmeric, rice flour or incense before use. For the night of the festival the mask is treated as the god itself. The photos here are from Palghar, across the border, where the tradition is best documented.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is living ritual theatre, older than any of the forts.
spotlights.memory_hook: For one night the mask is the god.

sections.title: Warli painting: a world in three shapes
sections.intro_md:
The best-known thing to come out of these hills is a way of drawing. **Warli painting**, made by the Warli of the border country between Maharashtra, Gujarat and Dadra and Nagar Haveli, uses white paste on dark mud walls and almost nothing but circles, triangles and lines. Traditionally it was women's ritual work: the wedding chauk with the mother goddess at its heart, painted fresh for each marriage.

From the 1970s it went out into the world on paper and canvas, carried by artists like **Jivya Soma Mashe**. Today it is everywhere from railway stations to T-shirts, and it holds a Geographical Indication tag. The spot-it test is simple: if a human is made of two triangles touching at a point, and the figures move in rings and spirals, it is Warli.

spotlights.name: Warli painting

where.label: Warli villages of the Maharashtra and Gujarat border

spotlights.spot_it: White figures made only of circles, triangles and lines on a red-brown mud wall: two triangles joined at the tips make a person; a spiral of them makes a tarpa dance.
spotlights.story_md: The Warli paint with a white paste of rice flour, water and gum, using a chewed bamboo twig as a brush, on walls plastered with mud. The grammar is tiny: a **circle** for the sun and moon, a **triangle** for mountains and trees, a **square** for a sacred enclosure. A human is two triangles meeting at a point. Women traditionally painted the wedding square, the chauk, with the goddess **Palghat** at its centre. In 1971 the All India Handicrafts Board sent the artist Bhaskar Kulkarni to the Warli to encourage painting on paper, and the art moved from walls to galleries. It received a Geographical Indication tag in 2014.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the most recognisable visual styles from India, and it began as ritual, not decoration.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two triangles make a person; a spiral of them makes a dance.

spotlights.name: Jivya Soma Mashe
spotlights.spot_it: His paintings are crowded and moving: hundreds of tiny figures in spirals and whorls, with a sense of wind and speed that older Warli walls rarely have.
spotlights.story_md: Warli painting had been made by women, for rituals. **Jivya Soma Mashe**, a Warli man from Dahanu, began in the 1970s to paint it for its own sake, on cloth and paper, with his son Balu. He turned the stick figure into a storyteller's tool, painting whole narratives of fishing, harvest, wedding and myth. His work travelled to exhibitions abroad, and he received the Padma Shri. Many art historians credit him with taking Warli painting from the village wall into the world art market. He died in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He changed Warli painting from ritual to art without losing its grammar.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who took the Warli wall to Paris.

sections.title: Migrants, Catholics and seafarers
sections.intro_md:
The territory's census numbers are some of the strangest in India. Between 2001 and 2011 Dadra and Nagar Haveli grew by **55.9%** and Daman district by **69%**, while India grew 17.7%. Almost all of that growth was migration into factory jobs, mostly by young men. So the sex ratio fell to **774** women per 1,000 men in Dadra and Nagar Haveli and **618** in Daman and Diu, the lowest in India. In Silvassa you hear Bhojpuri and Odia as often as Gujarati.

Underneath are much older communities. In Daman and Diu most people are Gujarati: in 2011 about **51%** spoke Gujarati and **36%** Hindi. A small Catholic community keeps Portuguese surnames and its own creole. Diu's **Kharwa** sailors have family on three continents, and people born in Portuguese Daman and Diu before 1961, with their descendants, have been able to claim Portuguese nationality, a door to Europe that many families have used.

spotlights.name: Silvassa's floating workforce
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of factory sheds, rented rooms of four or five men each, buses full of workers at shift change, and Bhojpuri, Odia and Marathi spoken in the bazaar.
spotlights.story_md: Silvassa, the old Portuguese town of Paço d'Arcos, had under 100,000 people in 2011, but the city's own figures add a floating population of more than **200,000** workers, mostly from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Odisha. Dadra and Nagar Haveli grew by **55.9%** between 2001 and 2011, and Daman district by **69%**, among the fastest rates in India. Because most migrants are young men who leave their families at home, the territory's sex ratio collapsed: **774 women per 1,000 men** in Dadra and Nagar Haveli and **618** in Daman and Diu in 2011. Daman and Diu's figure was the lowest in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows what tax-holiday industrialisation does to a small tribal district.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town where men outnumber women by three to two.

spotlights.name: Língua da Casa: the Portuguese of Daman and Diu
spotlights.spot_it: Heard, not seen: a Portuguese-based creole spoken at home by Catholic families in Daman and Diu, mixed with Gujarati and Konkani sounds.
spotlights.story_md: In some Damanese homes the family language is **Língua da Casa**, the house language, a Portuguese creole that descends from the Norteiro creole once spoken along the coast from Chaul and Vasai to Bombay and Daman. In 2010 it had roughly **4,000 native speakers in Daman** and only about **180 in Diu**, mostly Catholics. Diu's variety is listed as potentially endangered: young people switch to Gujarati, Hindi and English, and even the church is moving from Portuguese to English. Some speakers call it broken Portuguese; linguists call it a language.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the last living descendants of the Portuguese spoken along India's west coast.
spotlights.memory_hook: The house language of Daman, with 180 speakers left in Diu.

spotlights.name: The Kharwa seafarers of Diu
spotlights.spot_it: Hundreds of brightly painted wooden boats crammed into the harbour at Vanakbara, at the west end of Diu island, unloading fish at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: The **Kharwa** are Gujarat's hereditary sailors and shipbuilders. Kharwas from Diu and other Saurashtra ports crewed the Maratha navy in Shivaji's time and sailed dhows to Aden, Zanzibar and Singapore. Under Portuguese rule, Diu's Kharwas followed the empire's routes to **Mozambique**, and from there many later moved to **Lisbon**. Today the community runs the fishing fleet at Vanakbara, where the catch comes in between about 7 and 8 in the morning. Each year at Narial Purnima, the full moon of Shravan, they offer coconuts to the sea to reopen the sailing season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They link Diu to an Indian Ocean world that ran from East Africa to Southeast Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Diu to Mozambique to Lisbon, by boat and by family.

sections.title: Fish, dhokla, chouriço and the border bar
sections.intro_md:
The territory eats like the people who live in it. The coastal towns are fishing towns, and their kitchens run on the morning catch: prawn curries, grilled fish and squid. The Portuguese left a few dishes and habits, above all the spicy pork sausage **chouriço** and a taste for vinegar and grilling, but the majority table is Gujarati and vegetarian. Inland, the Adivasi table is rice, coarse millets such as kodri, and forest greens.

Then there is drink. Gujarat has been dry since 1960, and both Daman and Diu sit right on its border with legal, cheap liquor. For decades that has shaped the coastal economy as much as fishing: bars, beach shacks and weekend hotels full of visitors from Surat, Vapi and Ahmedabad.

spotlights.name: The morning catch at Vanakbara
spotlights.spot_it: Prawns, squid and fresh fish sold off the boats, then grilled or curried in the town's small restaurants.
spotlights.story_md: Both coastal districts are fishing towns first. In Diu the fleet comes into Vanakbara at first light and the catch is sold on the quay; in Daman boats line the Damanganga below the forts. Restaurant menus run on what came in: prawn curries, fried pomfret, squid and grilled fish. The Portuguese imprint shows less in recipes than in method, with vinegar, chilli, and a liking for grilled and roasted dishes. Gujarati vegetarian cooking, from thalis to dhokla, sits right beside it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Fishing still feeds and employs the coastal half of the territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: Breakfast is whatever came off the boat at seven.

spotlights.name: Dhokla and the Gujarati table
spotlights.spot_it: Spongy yellow squares of steamed gram-flour cake, topped with mustard seeds and green chillies, eaten with chutney at breakfast.
spotlights.story_md: Most people in Daman and Diu are Gujarati, and the everyday food is Gujarati: dhokla, khandvi, thepla, undhiyu in winter, and the full sweet-sour thali. In Dadra and Nagar Haveli the Adivasi table is different: rice and coarse millets such as kodri, with millet rotla and forest greens. Visitors who come for the bars of Daman often eat Gujarati vegetarian food two streets away.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The territory's food is a map of who lives here: Gujarati, Adivasi, Catholic and migrant.
spotlights.memory_hook: Beer on the beach, dhokla for breakfast.

spotlights.name: Daman's border bars
spotlights.spot_it: Cars with Gujarat number plates queued at the Daman checkpost on a Saturday evening, and beachfront bars along Devka.
spotlights.story_md: Gujarat has been dry since it was created in 1960. Daman sits on the Gujarat border and Diu is surrounded by it, and both sell liquor legally and cheaply. So for decades carloads of Gujarati men have crossed over in the evenings and weekends, mostly to the pubs and taverns of Nani Daman and the bars along Devka beach. The trade is large: Daman's excise department collected about **₹250 crore** in liquor revenue in 2016 to 2017. One MP even proposed merging Daman into Gujarat so that prohibition would apply. In December 2025 Gujarat itself relaxed rules for visitors at GIFT City.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a border can create an economy all by itself.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gujarat's dry law built Daman's wet weekends.

sections.title: The calendar: sea, harvest and freedom
sections.intro_md:
Three calendars run side by side here. The **fishing calendar** stops for the monsoon and restarts at **Narial Purnima** in August, when coconuts go into the sea. The **Adivasi calendar** follows rice: harvest dances in the season after the rains, Bhawada at Holi, Bohada masks in spring. The **Catholic calendar** of Daman and Diu brings feasts, Christmas, and Portuguese-style dances.

And there is the political calendar. The territory celebrates **2 August**, the day Silvassa was freed in 1954, and **19 December**, the day Daman and Diu were freed in 1961, alongside 15 August. Add Diwali, Navratri garba and Eid, and the beach festivals the tourism department stages each winter, and few places this small have so many reasons to hold a parade.

data.name: Narial Purnima; 2 August Liberation Day, DNH
Navratri garba; harvest and tarpa nights
19 December Liberation Day, Daman and Diu; Christmas; Festa de Diu

spotlights.name: Narial Purnima
spotlights.spot_it: Fishing families in their best clothes throwing coconuts into the sea, boats hung with flags and garlands for their first trip after the monsoon.
spotlights.story_md: Fishing stops through the monsoon, when the sea is too rough. At the full moon of Shravan, usually in August, the Kharwa and Koli fishing communities mark the reopening of the season. They offer coconuts, flowers and incense to Samudra, the sea, and pray to Ganesha for safe voyages. Boats are painted, decorated with flags and garlands, and taken out for the first time. The same day is Raksha Bandhan for much of north India, so in these towns sisters tie rakhis and fishermen feed the sea on the same morning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the calendar of a fishing economy, set by the monsoon.
spotlights.memory_hook: A coconut for the sea and the boats go out again.

spotlights.name: The two liberation days
spotlights.spot_it: Flag hoisting, parades and school pageants twice a year: on 2 August in Silvassa and on 19 December in Daman and Diu.
spotlights.story_md: The territory celebrates freedom on three dates. 15 August is shared with India. But **2 August** is Liberation Day in Dadra and Nagar Haveli, marking the fall of the Portuguese administration in 1954, and **19 December** is Liberation Day in Daman and Diu, marking the surrender of 1961, the same day as Goa's. A family in Silvassa therefore became Indian in practice seven years before one in Daman, though both were in India on the map in 1947.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reminds the rest of India that independence came in stages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three freedom days: 2 August, 15 August, 19 December.

sections.title: Where to go
sections.intro_md:
The territory is small enough to see in a long weekend, if you accept that its three districts are hours apart by road. **Diu** is the prize: the fort, Panikota, the churches, the old town through Zampa gate, the Khukri memorial, the Naida caves, Gangeshwar, and the beaches at **Nagoa** and **Ghoghla**. It has an airport with flights from Mumbai and Ahmedabad.

**Daman** is a day: Moti Daman's walls and churches, Nani Daman's fort, the lighthouse, and the beaches at **Devka** and **Jampore**. Inland, **Silvassa** and Nagar Haveli are for green and quiet: Vanganga lake, the deer park at Satmaliya, the lion safari at Vasona, and the Madhuban backwaters. October to March is the season; the monsoon is beautiful inland but closes the sea.

spotlights.name: Nagoa beach
spotlights.when: Year round, best October to March
spotlights.spot_it: A horseshoe of soft sand on Diu's south coast, sheltered by headlands, with hoka palms behind it and parasailing boats in front.
spotlights.story_md: Diu's most famous beach is a curving bay a few kilometres west of the town, near the airport. Its shape keeps the water calm for much of the year, which made it the island's main tourist beach: resorts, watersports, and crowds from Gujarat at weekends. Sunrise and sunset both work here, and the forked hoka palms make the skyline unlike any beach in Goa.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the beach that put Diu on Gujarat's holiday map.
spotlights.memory_hook: A horseshoe bay framed by forked palms.

spotlights.name: Ghoghla beach
spotlights.spot_it: A long, clean, quieter beach on the mainland side of the creek, with a Blue Flag pole at its entrance.
spotlights.story_md: Ghoghla is technically on the mainland, a part of Diu district across the creek from the island. It is the district's longest beach and holds an international **Blue Flag** certificate for water quality, safety and environmental management. The rocky shore nearby is full of life: limpets, snails and colonies of zoanthid soft coral in the tide pools.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the territory selling clean water rather than cheap beer.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Blue Flag on the side of Diu that is not an island.

spotlights.name: Devka and Jampore beaches, Daman
spotlights.spot_it: Grey-sand beaches with black rocks and big tides: Devka lined with hotels and a sea-front promenade, Jampore wider and emptier south of the river.
spotlights.story_md: Daman's coast is not a postcard Goa beach. The sand is grey, the tide goes out a long way, and the water near the river mouth is muddy. People come for the evening: Devka's promenade and its bars to the north of Nani Daman, and Jampore, south of Moti Daman, for wide flat sand and boats pulled up on the beach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the weekend playground of south Gujarat's industrial towns.
spotlights.memory_hook: Grey sand, long tides, crowded sunsets.

spotlights.name: Vanganga lake garden
spotlights.spot_it: A lake garden with bridges, islands and paddle boats, a few minutes from Dadra.
spotlights.story_md: Dadra and Nagar Haveli's tourism runs on gardens, lakes and forest drives. **Vanganga** near Dadra is a landscaped lake with bridges, lawns and boating, built for families from Vapi and Silvassa. Daman's equivalent is the **Mirasol lake garden** with fountains and islands. Further in are Dudhni lake, Khanvel's forest resorts and the deer park at Satmaliya.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how the territory has rebuilt itself as a weekend escape for nearby cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paddle boats in the old Portuguese enclave.

sections.title: How it earns: tax breaks, beer and sunshine
sections.intro_md:
Few places in India have been remade by policy as fast. In 1965 Dadra and Nagar Haveli got its first industrial estate and almost nothing happened: no railway, no skilled workers, no roads. In the 1980s the Centre offered a **15-year sales tax exemption** to draw industry to this backward district, and local industrialists say an **income tax holiday** followed in 1993. Plastics, textiles and consumer-goods plants followed, spilling over from the Vapi belt in Gujarat, and Daman's estates grew the same way. Today thousands of small and medium factories employ a floating migrant workforce, more than 200,000 around Silvassa alone, that outnumbers the town's own residents.

The coast lives on fishing, tourism and liquor excise, which brought Daman about **₹250 crore** in 2016 to 2017. And Diu has turned its sunshine into a selling point. Since 2018 it has met all its daytime power demand from solar.

data.label: Power imported from Gujarat before the solar park (up to)
Daytime demand met by renewables, 2018 onward

spotlights.name: The factory belt
spotlights.spot_it: Industrial estates of plastics and consumer-goods plants spreading along the roads from Vapi to Silvassa and Daman.
spotlights.story_md: Dadra and Nagar Haveli's first industrial estate opened in 1965, but almost nothing came. Then the Centre made the territory a tax haven for industry: a **15-year sales tax exemption** from the 1980s and, local industrialists say, an income tax holiday from 1993. Factories poured in, plastics above all, and Daman followed the same path. Wikipedia counts more than **3,500** small and medium units. The result is an industrial belt built on tax breaks, river water and migrant labour, sitting inside a tribal district.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a case study in what tax incentives can do, good and bad.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tax break turned forest villages into a factory belt.

spotlights.name: Diu's solar day
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of panels on 50 hectares of rocky ground and on government roofs, enough to run the whole island in daylight.
spotlights.story_md: Until 2017 Diu imported most of its power from Gujarat. Then it built a **9 MW** solar park on about **50 hectares** of barren rock and put panels on 79 government buildings. In April 2018 it became India's first smart city to meet **100% of its daytime demand** from renewable energy, and household tariffs were cut by 10% and then 15%. At night it still imports power. By 2025 the island's solar capacity was **11.88 MW**, including 2.88 MW on rooftops, and the Union renewable energy minister called it the first district to meet its daytime needs fully with solar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a small island can be a working model for clean power.
spotlights.memory_hook: By day, the sun runs the whole island.

spotlights.name: Diu and Daman airports
spotlights.spot_it: A small low terminal at Diu with flights to Mumbai and Ahmedabad; Daman's coast guard airfield now has a new civil terminal.
spotlights.story_md: Both Portuguese towns had their own airfields, since after 1954 the roads ran through hostile India. Diu's airfield was bombed in 1961; today it has flights to Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Surat and Goa, and a bridge ties the island to Gujarat's roads. Daman's airfield is the Indian Coast Guard's main air station on the west coast. On **5 June 2026** the Prime Minister opened a new civil terminal there, part of about ₹2,970 crore of projects.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Air links are how a scattered three-piece territory stays connected.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two colonial airstrips, now commuter airports.

sections.title: Who runs it
sections.intro_md:
A union territory without a legislature is governed directly from Delhi. The President appoints an **administrator**; there is no chief minister, no assembly and no state cabinet. Local democracy lives in municipal councils, district panchayats and the two Lok Sabha seats. That makes the administrator unusually powerful, and since 2016 that has been **Praful Khoda Patel**, a former Gujarat minister.

His years have brought airports, a medical college and hospital, new roads and a merged administration. They have also brought demolition drives against what the administration called encroachments, including in Daman in 2023, protests from fishing communities, and the 2021 death of Dadra and Nagar Haveli's long-time MP **Mohan Delkar**, whose note named the administrator.

spotlights.name: Praful Khoda Patel
spotlights.spot_it: A former Gujarat minister who runs the territory, and also Lakshadweep, with the powers of a governor and no elected assembly above him.
spotlights.story_md: Union territories without legislatures are run by an administrator appointed by the President. **Praful Khoda Patel**, a former BJP minister of state for home in Gujarat, has held Daman and Diu since August 2016, Dadra and Nagar Haveli since December 2016, the merged UT since 2020, and Lakshadweep as an extra charge since December 2020. His tenure brought fast building, including the NAMO medical college and hospital, new airports and roads, and also demolitions, protests and controversy. In 2021 the seven-time Dadra and Nagar Haveli MP **Mohan Delkar** died by suicide in Mumbai, leaving a note that named Patel; an FIR followed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shows how much power an unelected administrator holds in a UT without a legislature.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two territories, one administrator, no assembly.

spotlights.name: The Delkars of Dadra and Nagar Haveli
spotlights.spot_it: Seven Lok Sabha wins for one Adivasi leader, then his widow winning the seat under three different banners.
spotlights.story_md: **Mohan Delkar**, an Adivasi leader, won the Dadra and Nagar Haveli seat seven times, at different times for the Congress and the BJP, and in 2019 as an independent. After his death in February 2021, his widow **Kalaben Delkar** won the October 2021 by-election as a **Shiv Sena** candidate, beating the BJP by about 51,000 votes. In 2024 she switched to the BJP and won again, by 57,584 votes. In a territory with no assembly, its two MPs are the only elected voices above the panchayat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The seat shows how personal loyalty can matter more than party in small constituencies.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same family, three parties, one seat.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: the territory was always one place.** Fact: it is four separate Portuguese fragments, run as two UTs until 2020. Diu is about 200 km from Daman by sea and further by road.

**Myth: India took Dadra and Nagar Haveli by force in 1961.** Fact: it was freed by volunteers and police in 1954, ran itself for seven years, and joined India by agreement in 1961.

**Myth: Portuguese rule ended everywhere in 1961.** Fact: Portugal did not recognise the change until a treaty of 31 December 1974.

**Myth: the Naida caves were dug out for the fort.** Fact: it is a popular story; no study confirms it, and some say the caves are natural.

**Myth: the Pandavas installed Gangeshwar's lingas 5,500 years ago.** Fact: that is local tradition, not history.

**Myth: hoka palms grow only in Diu.** Fact: INTACH says so within India, but botanists dispute which species it is and where else it grows.

spotlights.name: Naida caves
spotlights.spot_it: A maze of sandstone chambers open to the sky, with tree roots hanging through the gaps and shafts of sunlight on the floor.
spotlights.story_md: Just outside the old town wall is a network of hollows, passages and roofless rooms in the soft rock. The popular story is that the Portuguese **quarried** the stone for Diu Fort here and left the caves behind. Some writers say they are natural, carved by erosion, and others say a mix. Another tale says Portuguese soldiers hid here in 1961. No archaeological study confirms any of these. What is certain is that the caves are among the most photographed places in the territory.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show how a good story attaches itself to any striking place.
spotlights.memory_hook: Did the fort come out of these caves? Nobody has proved it.

spotlights.name: Gangeshwar Mahadev
spotlights.spot_it: Five Shiva lingas in a rock hollow on the shore, which the sea covers and uncovers with every tide.
spotlights.story_md: At Fudam, about 3 km from Diu town, five lingas sit in a natural cave cut by the waves into black rock. At high tide only their tips show; at low tide pilgrims step down and pour water and flowers over them, and the sea washes the offerings away within minutes. Local belief says the five **Pandavas** installed them during their exile, one each, with Bhima's the largest. Some priests give a date of 5,500 years ago. That is tradition, not history, but the setting is real and remarkable.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a sacred site that the sea itself performs the ritual at.
spotlights.memory_hook: The sea does the abhishek twice a day.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**March 2025:** On 7 March the Prime Minister opened the 450-bed **NAMO hospital** in Silvassa, built for about ₹460 crore, with projects worth about ₹2,587 crore across the territory, from village roads to schools and water lines.

**May 2025:** On a visit by the Union renewable energy minister, Diu's solar capacity was reported at **11.88 MW**, and the island was called India's first district to meet its daytime needs fully with solar.

**December 2025:** Gujarat relaxed liquor rules for visitors at GIFT City, a small crack in the prohibition that built Daman's bar trade.

**5 June 2026:** The Prime Minister inaugurated a new terminal at Daman's **NAMO airport** and launched projects worth about ₹2,970 crore, including foundation stones for an iconic bridge, a convention centre and a **NIFT** campus.

**2026:** The territory remains without a legislature, with Praful Khoda Patel as administrator, a post he has held since 2016 and alongside Lakshadweep since 2020.

sections.title: Recap: the territory in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu is four fragments of Portuguese India, merged into one UT on 26 January 2020.
2. Its capital is Daman; its biggest town is Silvassa; it has 603 square km and about 5.87 lakh people (2011).
3. In 1509 a Portuguese fleet won the Indian Ocean in Diu's harbour.
4. Diu Fort survived Ottoman and Gujarati sieges in 1538 and 1546.
5. Nagar Haveli became Portuguese in 1783 as compensation for a damaged frigate.
6. It freed itself in 1954, ran as a de facto state for seven years, and joined India in 1961 through a one-day prime minister.
7. Daman and Diu were taken in Operation Vijay on 19 December 1961.
8. The Warli and their tarpa dance and painting are the inland district's heart.
9. Tax breaks made it a factory belt, with India's lowest sex ratio.
10. Diu now runs on sunlight by day, and Daman's new airport opened in 2026.

cards.front: What were the four pieces of the territory before 2020, and what joined them?
cards.back: Dadra, Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu; merged into one UT on 26 January 2020.

cards.front: Capital and largest town of the merged UT?
cards.back: Capital Daman; largest town Silvassa.

cards.front: Total area and 2011 population?
cards.back: About 603 square km; about 5.87 lakh people (2011).

cards.front: Name this fort and its year.
cards.back: Diu Fort, built from 1535 under a treaty with Bahadur Shah.

cards.front: What happened at Diu on 3 February 1509?
cards.back: Almeida's Portuguese fleet destroyed a Mamluk, Gujarati and Calicut fleet, winning control of the Indian Ocean trade.

cards.front: Whose death does this Akbarnama painting show?
cards.back: Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, who died off Diu in February 1537.

cards.front: Who besieged Diu in 1538 and failed?
cards.back: An Ottoman fleet under Hadim Suleiman Pasha, with Gujarat's army.

cards.front: Why did Portugal own Nagar Haveli?
cards.back: The Marathas handed over about 72 villages to compensate for the frigate Santana (treaty of 1779; possession 1783 and 1785).

cards.front: When was Dadra freed, and when did Dadra and Nagar Haveli join India formally?
cards.back: 22 July 1954 (Silvassa 2 August 1954); formally on 11 August 1961.

cards.front: Who was prime minister of Dadra and Nagar Haveli for one day?
cards.back: K. G. Badlani, IAS, on 11 August 1961, to sign the merger with Nehru.

cards.front: What did the World Court decide in 1960 about the enclaves?
cards.back: Portugal had a right of passage for civilians and goods but not for armed forces (8 to 7), and India had not broken the law.

cards.front: When were Daman and Diu freed?
cards.back: 19 December 1961, in Operation Vijay.

cards.front: This model remembers which ship, and what happened?
cards.back: INS Khukri, torpedoed off Diu on 9 December 1971; 194 men died, including Captain Mulla.

cards.front: Name this church and its date.
cards.back: St Paul's, Diu, completed 1610.

cards.front: Largest community of Dadra and Nagar Haveli, and its share of mother tongues in 1991?
cards.back: The Warli (Varli); 48.87% in the 1991 census.

cards.front: Name this dance and the instrument at its centre.
cards.back: The tarpa dance, around a gourd horn called the tarpa.

cards.front: Name this art and its three basic shapes.
cards.back: Warli painting: circle, triangle, square.

cards.front: Sex ratios in 2011 and why?
cards.back: Dadra and Nagar Haveli 774, Daman and Diu 618 (lowest in India), because of male migrant workers.

cards.front: What drew factories to Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman?
cards.back: Tax exemptions from the 1980s and 1990s, plus river water and migrant labour.

cards.front: What did Diu achieve in April 2018?
cards.back: First Indian smart city to run on 100% renewable power in daytime (9 MW solar park plus rooftops).

cards.front: Name this sea fort.
cards.back: Panikota (Fortim do Mar), Diu, later a prison.

cards.front: Name this fort and its river.

cards.front: Which fort's gate is this, and whose statue tops it?

cards.front: Name this carved town gate.

cards.front: Name these birds and the sanctuary.

cards.front: Which river is this, at Daman?
cards.back: The Damanganga, 131 km from the Sahyadri hills.

cards.front: Who is this viceroy, and what did he win in 1509?
cards.back: Francisco de Almeida; the Battle of Diu.

cards.front: Who is this, and what did he do in 1546?
cards.back: João de Castro, who relieved the second siege of Diu.

cards.front: This cruiser shelled Diu in 1961. What was her earlier name and battle?
cards.back: HMS Achilles; the Battle of the River Plate, 1939.

cards.front: Whose bust is this?

cards.front: Name this church in Moti Daman.
cards.back: Bom Jesus, consecrated 1603.

cards.front: What happens to the five lingas here?
cards.back: Gangeshwar, Diu: the tide covers them and washes away offerings.

cards.front: Name this masked festival.

cards.front: Whose style is this crowded spiral of figures?

cards.front: Name these caves and their popular legend.
cards.back: Naida caves, Diu; said, without proof, to be the quarry for Diu Fort.

cards.front: Name this beach.
cards.back: Nagoa, Diu.

cards.front: Daman's home creole is called Língua da ____.
cards.back: Casa (the house language).

cards.front: The tarpa is made from a dried ____.
cards.back: Bottle gourd.

cards.front: What is the hoka?
cards.back: A branching palm of Diu, related to Africa's doum palm; INTACH says the Portuguese brought it.

cards.front: How many Portuguese defended Diu in 1538?

cards.front: Where did many of Diu's Kharwa families migrate?

cards.front: Daman's liquor excise revenue in 2016 to 2017?
cards.back: About ₹250 crore.

cards.front: Lok Sabha seats of the merged UT, and its High Court?
cards.back: Two seats; the Bombay High Court.

cards.front: When did Portugal recognise Indian sovereignty over its former territories?
cards.back: By a treaty signed on 31 December 1974, after the Carnation Revolution.

cards.front: What did the PM open at Silvassa in March 2025?
cards.back: The 450-bed NAMO hospital, among about ₹2,587 crore of projects.

cards.front: Which is Diu Fort and which is Moti Daman?
cards.back: Diu Fort has the lighthouse on the sea; Moti Daman is the long walled town by the river.

cards.front: Name this museum building in Diu.
cards.back: St Thomas Church, now the Diu museum.

cards.front: What principle made the Right of Passage case famous in international law?
cards.back: That a local custom between just two states can create binding legal rights.

quiz_bank.prompt: Dadra and Nagar Haveli became part of India immediately after the Portuguese left in 1954.
quiz_bank.explanation: It was run as Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli by the Varishta Panchayat until it merged in August 1961.

quiz_bank.explanation: Surkhaab.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why did Francisco de Almeida attack the fleet at Diu in 1509?
quiz_bank.explanation: To avenge his son Lourenço, killed by the Mamluk fleet at Chaul in 1508.

quiz_bank.prompt: In 1538 an Ottoman fleet sent by Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Diu and failed.
quiz_bank.explanation: Hadim Suleiman Pasha besieged about 600 Portuguese for some four months and withdrew.

quiz_bank.prompt: How many bastions does Moti Daman fort have?
quiz_bank.explanation: Ten arrow-shaped bastions.

quiz_bank.prompt: What was Panikota, the fort in the sea at Diu, later used as?
quiz_bank.explanation: A prison, which is why it is called the sea jail.

quiz_bank.explanation: The United Front of Goans, led by Francis Mascarenhas and Viman Sardesai.

quiz_bank.prompt: What are the other two great churches of old Diu used for today?
quiz_bank.explanation: St Thomas is a museum and St Francis of Assisi became a hospital; only St Paul's is still a church.

quiz_bank.prompt: What happens to offerings at Gangeshwar temple in Diu?
quiz_bank.explanation: The sea washes them away: the five lingas sit in a tidal rock hollow.

quiz_bank.prompt: The tarpa is made mainly from what?
quiz_bank.explanation: A dried bottle gourd, with palm leaves, bamboo and wax.

quiz_bank.prompt: In the 1991 census, was Varli the mother tongue of more or less than 40% of the territory's people?
quiz_bank.explanation: 48.87%, by far the largest single language of Dadra and Nagar Haveli at the time.

quiz_bank.explanation: Two triangles joined at their tips, with a circle for the head.

quiz_bank.prompt: What is Língua da Casa?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Portuguese-based creole spoken at home by Catholic families in Daman and Diu.

quiz_bank.prompt: Daman's liquor trade exists largely because neighbouring Gujarat is dry.
quiz_bank.explanation: Gujarat has had prohibition since 1960; Daman's excise revenue was about ₹250 crore in 2016 to 2017.

quiz_bank.explanation: Coconuts, with flowers and incense, to reopen the sailing season after the monsoon.

quiz_bank.prompt: What mainly drew factories to Dadra and Nagar Haveli?
quiz_bank.explanation: Tax exemptions: a 15-year sales tax exemption from the 1980s and an income tax holiday from 1993.

quiz_bank.prompt: On which party's ticket did Kalaben Delkar win the 2021 by-election?
quiz_bank.explanation: Shiv Sena. She later joined the BJP and won again in 2024.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which beach in the territory holds an international Blue Flag certificate?
quiz_bank.explanation: Ghoghla, on the mainland part of Diu district.

quiz_bank.explanation: A new terminal at Daman's NAMO airport, part of about ₹2,970 crore of projects.

side_dish.title: How two forest villages made international law
side_dish.body_md:
Lawyers who have never heard of Silvassa know the case it caused. When India blocked Portuguese access to Dadra and Nagar Haveli in 1954, Portugal went to the **International Court of Justice** in December 1955, arguing that it had a **right of passage** across Indian territory to reach its enclaves.

The hard question was where such a right could come from. There was no modern treaty. Portugal pointed to more than a century of practice: the British, and the Marathas before them, had let Portuguese officials and goods move freely between Daman and the villages. India argued that a custom needs many states, not two, to become law.

In April 1960 the Court sided with Portugal on that principle and against it on the facts that mattered. It held that **a local custom between just two states can create binding rights**, a point now taught in every course on the sources of international law. It found that such a custom did exist for private persons, civil officials and goods. But for **armed forces, armed police and weapons** there had always been a need for permission, so no right existed, by a single vote, 8 to 7. And India had not broken the law by suspending passage in the tense conditions of 1954.

The lesson reaches beyond colonial history. Rights can grow out of how neighbours behave over a long time, not only out of what they sign. But the Court also showed how carefully it reads that behaviour: the line it drew was between a postman and a soldier.

offline_task.title: Find the Portuguese in your own kitchen
offline_task.body_md:
Portugal left Daman and Diu in 1961, but it left words in almost every Indian language. Today, find at least five of them in your own home and say each out loud with its Portuguese parent.

- **Pav** (bread roll) from *pão*.
- **Chabi** (key) from *chave*.
- **Almirah** (cupboard) from *armário*.
- **Balti** (bucket) from *balde*.
- **Kaju** (cashew) from *caju*.
- **Ananas** (pineapple) from *ananás*.
- **Mistri** (skilled workman) from *mestre*.
- **Tauliya** (towel) from *toalha*.
- **Girja** (church) from *igreja*.

Then do one more step: ask an older relative which of these words they grew up with, and which ones they think are 'Hindi' or 'Gujarati' words. Most people are surprised how many came off Portuguese ships. Write down any other word you suspect, and check it tomorrow.

best_facts.fact: To sign Dadra and Nagar Haveli into India, an IAS officer, K. G. Badlani, was made its prime minister for one day, 11 August 1961.
best_facts.why_surprising: A civil servant was a head of government for 24 hours.

best_facts.fact: Portugal got Nagar Haveli not by conquest but as compensation from the Marathas for the frigate Santana, damaged in 1772.
best_facts.why_surprising: A border drawn by an insurance claim.

best_facts.fact: The World Court ruled 8 votes to 7 in 1960 that Portugal could not march armed forces across India to its enclaves.
best_facts.why_surprising: One judge's vote settled a colonial dispute.

best_facts.fact: The cruiser that shelled Diu in December 1961, INS Delhi, had fought the Graf Spee at the River Plate in 1939 as HMS Achilles.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Second World War veteran ended Portuguese India.

best_facts.fact: The 1509 Battle of Diu, fought out of a father's revenge for his son, gave Portugal control of the Indian Ocean for about a century.
In 1538 the Ottoman Empire sent its governor of Egypt, a 60-year-old eunuch, with dozens of ships to take Diu; about 600 defenders held out for four months.
best_facts.why_surprising: The Ottomans fought the Portuguese in Gujarat.

best_facts.fact: In 2011 Daman and Diu had 618 women for every 1,000 men, the lowest in India, because its factories run on young male migrants.
best_facts.why_surprising: A sex ratio shaped by tax policy.

best_facts.fact: In 1991, Varli was the mother tongue of 48.87% of Dadra and Nagar Haveli; by 2011 Adivasis were only about 52% of a population that had more than doubled.
best_facts.why_surprising: Factories rewrote the territory's demography in two decades.

best_facts.fact: INS Khukri, sunk off Diu on 9 December 1971 with 194 men, is the Indian Navy's worst single loss of life since independence; her captain went down with her.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's naval tragedy happened off a holiday island.

best_facts.fact: In April 2018 Diu became India's first smart city to meet all its daytime power demand from renewable energy.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tiny island beat the big cities to it.

best_facts.fact: Bahadur Shah of Gujarat let the Portuguese build Diu Fort to fight the Mughals, then died in the sea off Diu in 1537 while negotiating with them.
best_facts.why_surprising: The host drowned and the guests stayed 424 years.

best_facts.fact: About 180 people in Diu still speak a Portuguese-based creole at home, against roughly 4,000 in Daman.
At Gangeshwar in Diu, five Shiva lingas sit in a tidal rock pool, and the sea washes away the offerings.
